result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.jaccard_coefficient()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute Jaccard coefficient for node pairs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L10878-L10935){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.jaccard_coefficient(ebunch=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Jaccard coefficient](/assets/graphs/jaccard-coefficient.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Nodes B and E are outlined in the accent color with their shared neighbors C and D filled in accent. A table scores three requested pairs by shared over total distinct neighbors: B, E is 2 of 5 = 0.4, C, D is 2 of 3 = 0.67, and A, E is 0." width="100%"} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, computes `|N(u) ∩ N(v)| / |N(u) ∪ N(v)|`, which is the ratio of common neighbors to total distinct neighbors. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of node pairs to compute predictions for. Each pair can use node IDs (integers) or labels (strings). If `None`, computes for all pairs of nodes that are not already connected. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, coefficient)` tuples where coefficient is the Jaccard similarity. Results are returned with node IDs. Coefficient is `0.0` if both nodes have no neighbors. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Jaccard coefficient normalizes common neighbors by the total distinct neighbors of the two nodes: $J(u, v) = \dfrac{|N(u) \cap N(v)|}{|N(u) \cup N(v)|} \in [0, 1]$, with $1$ signalling identical neighborhoods and $0$ meaning no overlap. The normalization makes it fairer than raw common-neighbor counts when comparing pairs with very different degrees, at the cost of inflating scores for low-degree pairs (two isolated leaves that share their only neighbor score a perfect $1$). Cost is $O(k)$ per pair. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 5-node path, nodes two hops apart (like `1` and `3`) share exactly one neighbor out of two total distinct neighbors, giving a coefficient of `0.5`: ::: {#fc271228 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_path_graph(5) # 1-2-3-4-5 graph.jaccard_coefficient([(1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 4)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(1, 3, 0.5), (1, 4, 0.0), (2, 4, 0.3333333333333333)] ``` ::: :::
